questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design extensible, runtime-extendable components with minimal coupling using Strategy + Registry patterns.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy: encapsulate evaluation logic per flag
- Registry/Plugin: dynamic, runtime-extensible factories
- Dependency Injection: decouples engine from evaluators
- Thread-safety and versioning considerations for runtime extensions

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Context { tenantId: string; userId: string; region?: string; [key: string]: any }
interface Evaluator { evaluate(ctx: Context): boolean }
interface EvaluatorFactory { create(): Evaluator }
class Registry { private map = new Map<string, EvaluatorFactory>(); register(n: string, f: EvaluatorFactory) { this.map.set(n, f) } getFactory(n: string): EvaluatorFactory | undefined { return this.map.get(n) } }
class FlagEngine { constructor(private registry: Registry) {} isEnabled(flag: string, ctx: Context): boolean { const f = this.registry.getFactory(flag); if (!f) throw new Error(`Unknown flag: ${flag}`); return f.create().evaluate(ctx); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle hot-reload of strategies without restarting the service?
- How would you version/evolve evaluator interfaces while keeping backward compatibility?

## Why This Is Asked
Explores designing an extensible rate limiter with runtime algorithm plug-ins for a high-scale gateway.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy + Registry for runtime extensibility
- Per-endpoint quotas and per-key isolation
- Clock abstraction for testability and skew handling

## Code Example

```javascript
interface Algorithm {
  shouldPass(key: string, now: number): boolean
  record(key: string, now: number): void
}
class Registry { register(name: string, factory: ()=>Algorithm): void; get(name:string): ()=>Algorithm }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure thread-safety and lock-free reads for high throughput?
- How would you test time-based behavior and simulate clock skew?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests ability to build a safe, extensible plugin pipeline for high-throughput payments, focusing on runtime extensibility, isolation, and concurrency control.

## Key Concepts

- Pipeline pattern
- Registry/plugin system
- Stateless processors
- Per-event isolation
- Concurrency and backpressure

## Code Example

```typescript
interface Event { id: string; payload: any }
interface Processor { process(e: Event): Promise<Event> }
type Factory = () => Processor
class Registry { register(name: string, f: Factory): void; create(name: string): Processor | null }
```

```
// Minimal usage
const reg = new Registry()
reg.register('audit', () => new AuditProcessor())
reg.register('enrich', () => new EnrichProcessor())
reg.register('risk-check', () => new RiskCheckProcessor())

async function handleEvent(e: Event) {
  const names = ['audit', 'enrich', 'risk-check']
  const pipeline = names.map(n => reg.create(n)!).filter(Boolean)
  let ev = e
  for (const p of pipeline) {
    ev = await p.process(ev)
  }
  return ev
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you enforce per-event isolation if processors mutate payload in place?
- What strategies would you use to implement backpressure when the registry contains many heavy processors?
